newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-Gandhi's old home is still a quiet haven.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Gandhi's old home is still a quiet haven.

text.p: When American civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. visited Bombay in 1959, he spurned the swanky Taj Mahal Hotel and insisted on staying in a simple house tucked away on a quiet and leafy lane.

There, he hoped to find inspiration from the one-time home of his mentor -- Mahatma Gandhi, the spiritual father of India's independence and champion of those who lived on the bottom rung of Hinduism's long social ladder.
"He felt that he would not be able to derive good vibrations by just a brief visit. He just had to spend the night at Mani Bhavan," says Gandhi's grand-daughter, Usha Gokani.
Ironically, 20 years after Gandhi was shot dead at a prayer meeting in 1948, King himself was gunned down on the balcony of a Memphis hotel.

For tourists today, exhausted by the hurly-burly of India's commercial powerhouse and dispirited by its grim shanty-towns, a visit to the haven of Mani Bhavan and its Gandhi museum is a breath of fresh air.
UNSPECTACULAR BUT HISTORICAL HOUSE
An unspectacular house named after its original owner, Mani Bhavan was home from 1917 to 1934 for the thin, bespectacled ascetic whose banner was truth, morality and non-violence.
Those years, when he stayed there as a guest of a jeweller called Manilal Jhaveri, were perhaps the most critical of India's independence movement.
It was from there that Gandhi launched his first non-violent resistance against the Rowlatt Act of 1919, with which India's British colonial masters aimed to gag the press.

And it was from there, in the same year, that the first Non-Cooperation Movement was launched to vent public outrage at the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh, when troops fired for 10 minutes into a crowd, killing at least 379 people.

"Every time Gandhi stayed here on the second floor...it would be a beehive of activity," says Pushpa Ohol, the longest-serving official of the Bombay Gandhi Memorial Trust, a non-government organisation headquartered at Mani Bhavan.

Visitors included independent India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, the founder and first president of Pakistan, Mohammed Ali Jinnah, and the lower-caste Hindu leader and architect of India's constitution, B.R. Ambedkar.
REMEMBRANCE OF A FRUGAL LIFE
The ground floor contains a library of more than 50,000 books, many on Gandhi and his thought. The upper floors have been converted into a museum.
Gandhi's own room speaks volumes about the frugal life he led. Inside there is a thin mattress, a pillow, a low writing desk, an antique telephone and some spinning wheels.

"My grandfather learned how to card and spin cotton at Mani Bhavan," says Gokani. "And to this day we have a professional carder who visits once a week, to instruct those interested in learning this skill."
Though a memorial to Gandhi, time doesn't stand still at Mani Bhavan. Today, it is a living testimony to his beliefs.

"Mani Bhavan today serves two important functions," explains Gandhian and freedom fighter Usha Mehta. "As a memorial to Gandhi, we have tried to give visitors and students some idea of Gandhi's ideology and vision for independent India."
"Secondly, we have opened an Institute of Research on Gandhian Thought and Rural Development."
THESES ON GANDHIAN THOUGHT

Affiliated with Bombay University, the institute prepares students for theses on Gandhian thought and rural development. At grass-roots level, it trains people in low-cost, labour-intensive agricultural and industrial technologies.
The common thread of Gandhi and his ideology runs through a host of other activities hosted by Mani Bhavan.
There are annual competitions for school students in painting, elocution, recitation, and play-acting, all drawing their themes from the Freedom Struggle, Gandhi and Gandhism.
"All these activities are geared to keeping Gandhi alive in spirit," says Gokani.
The greatest tribute, however, to Gandhi's memory was a freedom march on August 9 to mark the anniversary of the Quit India Movement of 1942.
The procession kicked off a year of events in Bombay to mark the Golden Jubilee of Indian Independence, which was declared on August 15, 1947.
